title: Grade 2 Maths Homework: A Parent's Survival Guide (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: Grade 2 Maths Homework: A Parent's Guide + Quiz
meta_desc: Help with Grade 2 maths homework the smart way: what it covers, a stress-free routine, quick wins for regrouping and tables, plus a free quiz.
excerpt: Grade 2 maths homework is where the tears usually start — carrying, tables, word problems all land in one year. Here is how to help your child without doing it for them, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
It is 7 pm, the maths homework sheet says ‘47 + 38’, and your Class 2 child has written 715. You know it is wrong. They are certain it is right. And the honest problem is that most of us were never taught how to help — we just did the sum ourselves and moved on. That is exactly the trap. Grade 2 maths homework is the first year where the maths stops being obvious to adults too, and how you handle these evenings shapes whether your child grows up thinking they are ‘good at maths’ or not.

I have sat with a lot of seven-year-olds over homework, and the pattern is always the same: the child does not need you to solve it, they need you to slow it down. This guide covers what Grade 2 maths homework actually contains, how to help without hijacking, a routine that keeps the peace, and the two or three moments when you genuinely should worry.

What Grade 2 maths homework actually covers

The NCERT-aligned Class 2 syllabus jumps a long way from Grade 1. Your child moves from counting to real operations, and the homework follows. Expect sheets on:

  • Addition and subtraction with regrouping — carrying and borrowing across the tens, the single biggest source of homework mistakes.
  • Place value to 1000 — hundreds, tens and ones, and reading numbers in words.
  • Multiplication tables — usually the 2, 5 and 10 times tables, taught as repeated addition first.
  • Word problems — two or three lines of text that hide a sum inside a story.
  • Money, time and measurement — rupees and paise, telling time to the half-hour, and comparing lengths and weights.

The tables and the regrouping are where families get stuck. Everything else is usually a matter of practice.

How to help without doing it for them

The rule I give every parent: your pencil never touches the paper. The moment you write the answer, the learning transfers to you, not your child. Instead, help with your voice.

Ask, do not tell

When a sum is wrong, resist ‘no, it’s 85’. Ask ‘how many tens are in 47? and in 38?’ A question hands the thinking back to the child. Telling closes it down. It is slower — painfully so on a Tuesday night — but it is the whole point.

Make it concrete first

If regrouping is not clicking on paper, drop the paper. Grab a fistful of coins or beans and physically make ten ones into a ten. A child who has moved ten objects into a bundle understands carrying in a way no explanation on paper delivers. Come back to the digits afterwards.

Let them be wrong for a minute

Watching your child head toward a wrong answer is uncomfortable, and the instinct to jump in is strong. Don’t. A mistake they catch themselves teaches more than a correct answer you handed over. Give it a beat.

A stress-free homework routine

Grade 2 homework should take about 20 minutes. If it is regularly eating an hour with tears, the problem is rarely the child — it is usually the setup. A routine that works for the parents I know:

StepWhat to doWhy it helps
Same time, same spotA fixed 20-minute slot, not right after schoolRemoves the daily ‘when’ argument; a snack and a break first resets a tired brain
Read it togetherRead the instruction aloud once, then let them startHalf of ‘wrong’ answers are misread questions, not maths errors
You sit near, not overBe within reach but do something of your ownSignals independence while keeping help available
Stop at 20 minutesEnd on time even if unfinished; note it for the teacherProtects the child’s relationship with maths; the teacher needs to know it took too long

Quick wins for the hard topics

Three targeted fixes solve most Grade 2 homework battles.

Regrouping: name the carry out loud

For 47 + 38, say it as a story: ‘7 and 8 is 15 — that’s one ten and five, so I write the 5 and carry the ten’. The word ‘carry’ should be said, not just written as a tiny 1. Children who narrate the carry stop losing it.

Tables: chant them, don’t test them

The 2, 5 and 10 tables go in through rhythm long before they go in through drilling. Chant the 5 table on the walk to school. Skip-count by 2s while climbing stairs. Save the written quiz for after the chant is automatic — testing a table your child has not yet memorised just teaches them they are bad at it.

Word problems: circle the numbers, underline the question

Teach one habit: circle every number, underline the actual question, then decide — is this a ‘put together’ (add) or a ‘take away / how many more’ (subtract) story? That two-pen ritual turns a wall of text into a solvable sum.

When to actually worry

Most Grade 2 wobbles are normal. A few are worth a quiet word with the teacher:

  • Homework consistently takes far longer than 20 minutes despite a good routine.
  • Your child still counts on fingers for 3 + 4 well into the year — number bonds have not formed.
  • They reverse or scramble digits (writing 52 as 25) most of the time, not occasionally.
  • Real distress — tears or ‘I’m stupid’ — around maths specifically.

None of these mean disaster. They mean your child needs a different kind of practice, sooner rather than later. Flag it early; Grade 2 gaps are cheap to fix and expensive to ignore.

Try the quiz, then practise on paper

Below is a free 8-question quiz pitched exactly at Grade 2 — regrouping, tables, place value and a word problem or two. Let your child work through it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When you want structured written practice, the printable Class 2 workbook at the end gives graded worksheets with answer keys, so homework night has a plan instead of a panic.

quiz.intro: Eight questions covering regrouping, tables, place value and word problems. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 2 maths: regrouping, tables, place value and word problems

questions.explanation: 7 + 8 = 15, so write 5 and carry 1 ten. Then 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. The answer is 85.
You cannot take 7 from 2, so borrow a ten: 12 − 7 = 5, then 5 − 2 = 3. The answer is 35.

questions.q: In the number 356, what is the value of the digit 3?
questions.explanation: The 3 is in the hundreds place, so its value is 300.
7 × 2 means seven taken two times, which is 7 + 7 = 14.

questions.q: Riya had 45 stickers and gave 18 to her friend. How many are left?
questions.explanation: This is a take-away story: 45 − 18. Borrow a ten: 15 − 8 = 7, then 3 − 1 = 2. She has 27 left.

questions.q: What is 300 + 50 + 6 written as one number?
A shop sells pencils in packs of 10. How many pencils are in 4 packs?
questions.explanation: 4 packs of 10 is 10 + 10 + 10 + 10, which is 4 × 10 = 40 pencils.

faq.q: How long should Grade 2 maths homework take?
faq.a: Around 20 minutes. If it regularly stretches past that despite a calm routine, the sheet is too hard or the concept has not landed yet — note it and tell the teacher, rather than forcing your child through an hour of frustration.

faq.q: My child keeps getting regrouping wrong. What do I do?
faq.a: Put the pencil down and use real objects. Have them physically bundle ten coins or beans into a group of ten, so ‘carrying’ becomes something they can see and touch. Once the idea is concrete, the written method follows quickly.

faq.q: Should I correct every mistake as it happens?
faq.a: No. Let your child finish a section, then review it together and ask questions like ‘how many tens are here?’ instead of giving the answer. A mistake they find and fix themselves teaches far more than one you correct for them.

faq.q: How do I help my child learn the times tables?
faq.a: Chant before you test. Skip-count the 2, 5 and 10 tables aloud on the walk to school or up the stairs until the rhythm is automatic. Written table tests only work once the chant is already in memory.
